A major NHS hospital trust has declared a critical incident amid rising flu and COVID cases, long A&E waiting times and increasing pressure on emergency services.


## NHS Hospital Declares Critical Incident Amid Rising Flu and COVID Cases


Pressure on England's healthcare system is increasing as another major NHS hospital trust declares a critical incident following a surge in demand for emergency services.


University Hospitals of Derby and Burton NHS Foundation Trust (UHDB) has announced the critical incident after its emergency departments experienced overwhelming demand, resulting in significant delays for patients seeking urgent medical attention.


The situation highlights growing concerns about NHS winter pressures, particularly as seasonal respiratory illnesses, including influenza and COVID-19, continue to place additional strain on hospitals.


Royal Derby Hospital is reportedly experiencing some of the most severe pressures, with average Accident and Emergency (A&E) waiting times reaching approximately nine hours.


Hospital leaders have urged the public to use emergency departments responsibly and seek alternative healthcare services for conditions that are not life-threatening.


## Flu and COVID Cases Add to NHS Hospital Pressures


According to the trust, rising cases of seasonal respiratory infections are contributing significantly to the increased demand for hospital services.


Royal Derby Hospital was reported to be treating approximately 67 patients with flu and 24 patients with confirmed COVID-19 at the time of the announcement.


These infections are adding to existing pressures, with hospitals facing increased admissions and difficulties maintaining patient flow through emergency departments.


Winter traditionally brings additional challenges for the NHS, as colder weather and circulating respiratory viruses contribute to higher demand for healthcare.


Patients requiring hospital treatment can also experience longer stays when beds become unavailable, creating further difficulties for emergency departments.


The latest situation in Derby and Burton demonstrates how quickly seasonal illnesses can affect hospital capacity and the delivery of essential services.


## NHS Urges Public to Avoid Unnecessary A&E Visits


Hospital management has asked members of the public to attend A&E only when dealing with serious or life-threatening medical emergencies.


People experiencing less urgent health problems are being encouraged to consider other NHS services, including:


- NHS 111 for medical advice and guidance.
- GP practices for non-emergency health concerns.
- Local pharmacies for advice about minor illnesses and common conditions.
- Urgent treatment centres for conditions requiring prompt but non-emergency attention.


These services can help patients receive appropriate medical support while reducing unnecessary pressure on hospital emergency departments.


However, anyone experiencing a medical emergency should not delay seeking help. People who believe they are facing a life-threatening emergency should call 999 or attend an emergency department.


The trust has also asked families and carers to arrange the collection of relatives who have been medically assessed and are ready to leave hospital.


This is intended to help free up beds for patients who urgently need admission.


## Hospital Introduces Additional Support to Manage Demand


Jo Wright, interim executive chief operating officer at UHDB, acknowledged the significant pressures facing hospital teams.


She explained that additional clinical support was being directed towards areas experiencing the greatest demand.


The trust is also working with wider healthcare partners to improve patient movement through hospitals and support people who are ready for discharge.


Despite declaring a critical incident, hospital leaders stressed that emergency services remain available to patients who genuinely need urgent medical care.


A critical incident is an operational measure that allows NHS organisations to request and coordinate additional support across the wider healthcare system.


It does not mean that hospitals have closed or that emergency treatment has stopped.


Instead, it signals that normal operational capacity is under significant pressure and additional measures may be required to maintain safe patient care.


Patients with existing appointments have also been advised to continue attending unless they are contacted directly and told otherwise.


## Nottingham Hospitals Also Experience Significant Pressure


The situation is not limited to Derbyshire.


Nearby Nottingham is also experiencing considerable pressure on its hospital services, with Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust reporting a sharp increase in flu and COVID cases.


The trust has highlighted sustained pressure on services and high numbers of hospital admissions.


Patients attending Queen's Medical Centre and Nottingham City Hospital have reportedly experienced lengthy delays.


Some patients have also faced extended waits in ambulances outside hospital emergency departments, with reported delays reaching up to four hours.


These developments raise further concerns about the ability of emergency services to manage increasing demand during the winter period.


The challenges facing hospitals across the Midlands demonstrate the wider impact of respiratory illnesses on healthcare capacity.


## NHS Waiting Times Highlight Growing Concerns


The latest NHS performance figures also reveal the extent of the challenges facing emergency care in England.


Monthly NHS statistics released earlier in November 2026 showed that approximately 2.5 million people attended A&E departments during October.


This represented the highest monthly attendance figure recorded at the time.


The figures also indicated that more than 3,500 patients each day received hospital care in corridors or other temporary treatment spaces during October.


Meanwhile, nearly 58,000 patients reportedly waited more than 12 hours for a hospital bed after the decision to admit them.


Long delays in receiving an inpatient bed are a serious concern because they can affect patient safety, treatment outcomes and the overall quality of care.


The growing number of patients requiring emergency treatment, combined with limited hospital capacity, continues to create challenges for NHS organisations.


## How Can People Protect Themselves During the Flu Season?


With flu and COVID-19 contributing to increasing hospital admissions, taking sensible precautions can help reduce the risk of infection and protect vulnerable people.


Health professionals generally recommend the following measures:


**1. Consider eligible vaccinations**


People who are eligible for NHS flu and COVID-19 vaccinations should consider taking up the offer. Vaccination can reduce the risk of serious illness and hospitalisation.


**2. Maintain good hand hygiene**


Regular handwashing with soap and water can help reduce the spread of respiratory infections and other viruses.


**3. Stay home when unwell**


People experiencing symptoms of respiratory infections should try to avoid close contact with vulnerable individuals and follow current public health advice.


**4. Seek medical advice when necessary**


Anyone concerned about worsening symptoms should contact an appropriate healthcare professional. NHS 111 can provide guidance about the next steps.


**5. Take extra care around vulnerable people**


Older adults, people with certain long-term health conditions and individuals with weakened immune systems may face a greater risk of complications from respiratory infections.


Taking reasonable precautions can help protect both individuals and the wider community.


## NHS Winter Crisis Raises Questions About Hospital Capacity


The declaration of a critical incident at University Hospitals of Derby and Burton comes amid wider concerns about the ability of NHS hospitals to cope with increasing demand.


Rising flu and COVID cases, lengthy A&E waits, ambulance delays and limited bed availability are creating significant operational challenges.


Although hospitals are introducing additional support and working with healthcare partners, the situation underlines the importance of protecting emergency services and ensuring patients receive the right care in the right setting.


For members of the public, following NHS guidance, using alternative healthcare services when appropriate and taking steps to reduce infection risks can all help ease pressure on hospitals.


As winter progresses, the ability of healthcare services to manage seasonal illness and emergency admissions will remain an important issue for patients and NHS staff across England.
